title: 4. Daily regimen and fills
text:
Mark dispense days
A drug in today’s regimen that was dispensed today counts as a 30-pill fill. A drug dispensed that is not in the current regimen does not count, which is how the original handled stray fills of old drugs.

# A drug in the current regimen that was filled that day counts as 30 pills.
dispensed_drugs <- fills |>
  distinct(studyid, date = dispense_date, drug_name = drugname) |>
  mutate(pills_dispensed = fill_size_pills)

daily_drugs <- daily_drugs |>
  left_join(dispensed_drugs, by = c("studyid", "date", "drug_name")) |>
  mutate(pills_dispensed = coalesce(pills_dispensed, 0))

title: Methodological background
text: General ideas this kind of analysis rests on. What this study chose is on Study design and methods.

title: Methodological background
section: Pharmacy fills as a record of treatment
text:
Pharmacy fills as a record of treatment
A clinic pharmacy records each dispensing: the patient, the date, the product and (usually) the quantity. Fills tell you what a patient collected, not what they swallowed, but they are recorded the same way for everyone and cover every day. Two things have to be worked out from them:

Which regimen a patient is on. A regimen is the set of drugs filled together. Patients sometimes pick up the drugs of one regimen on different days, refill one drug and not another, or keep collecting an old drug after a switch, so a rule such as “the drugs filled on the same day make the regimen” needs checking against the record.
Whether a patient has medication on hand. If each fill is assumed to last a fixed number of days, pills on hand can be counted forward day by day: a fill adds pills, each day uses one, and an early refill adds to what is left. A day is covered when every drug in the regimen is on hand. The proportion of days covered (PDC) over a period is a standard adherence measure; 80% is the conventional cut-off. It is a lower bound when patients can also fill elsewhere.

title: Methodological background
section: One row per person per day
text:
One row per person per day
Fills, labs and visits happen on irregular dates. Expanding each patient to one row per calendar day puts everything on the same time line: on any day you can ask what regimen the patient was on, how many pills they had, and what their most recent viral load was (the last value carried forward), and how long until the next test. Counting days, quarters or years from a start date then becomes simple filtering. The cost is size: a few thousand patients over six years is millions of rows, which mattered for Stata in 2014 and matters much less in R today.

title: Methodological background
text:
Retention and viral suppression
Retention in care is usually measured by contacts with care separated by enough time within a year. The US Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) HIV/AIDS Bureau’s performance measures count medical visits at least 90 days apart; studies working from laboratory data often use viral load tests as the marker of a visit. Viral suppression is defined by a threshold, which depends on what the laboratory assay can detect: older assays reported down to 400 copies/mL, newer ones to 50 or 20.

title: Methodological background
section: Propensity scores and inverse probability weights
text:
Propensity scores and inverse probability weights
In an observational study the groups being compared differ in ways that also affect the outcome. A propensity score is each person’s probability of receiving the treatment given their measured characteristics, estimated with a logistic regression. Weighting each person by the inverse of the probability of the treatment they actually received (inverse probability of treatment weighting, IPTW) creates a pseudo-population in which the measured characteristics are balanced between groups, and the weighted comparison estimates the average treatment effect. Because weights are estimated and some are large, standard errors need a robust (sandwich) estimator. Weighting balances only what was measured: unmeasured confounding remains.

title: Methodological background
text:
Reporting
Observational studies using routinely collected data are reported following STROBE and its extension RECORD (Elm et al. 2007; Benchimol et al. 2015).

title: 3. One row per patient-day
3. One row per patient-day
text:
Carry values forward and back
Stata counted days since the last test with a running sum (replace x = 1 + x[_n-1] if x==.), then sorted the data by negative date and repeated the trick to count days until the next test. tidyr::fill() carries a value down (or up) to the following missing rows, so the date of the last test and of the next test can be filled and subtracted from today’s date. The same fill gives the last value carried forward (LVCFCD4, LVCFViralLoad) and the next value (NextCD4, NextViralLoad).
Days before a patient’s first test have no “last” value; days after the last test have no “next” one. That second fact defines “still in care” in step 5.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Last value carried forward (filled down) and next value (filled up), with the
# dates they come from, so that days since the last test and days until the
# next one can be counted. Before a patient's first test the "last" values are
# missing; after the last test the "next" values are missing.
person_days <- person_days |>
  mutate(
    last_cd4_date = if_else(is.na(current_cd4), as.Date(NA), date),
    last_vl_date = if_else(is.na(current_vl), as.Date(NA), date),
    lvcf_cd4 = current_cd4,
    lvcf_vl = current_vl,
    next_cd4_date = last_cd4_date,
    next_vl_date = last_vl_date,
    next_cd4 = current_cd4,
    next_vl = current_vl
  ) |>
  arrange(studyid, date) |>
  group_by(studyid) |>
  fill(last_cd4_date, last_vl_date, lvcf_cd4, lvcf_vl, .direction = "down") |>
  fill(next_cd4_date, next_vl_date, next_cd4, next_vl, .direction = "up") |>
  ungroup()

The gap is the number of days between the tests either side of a day.

    days_since_last_cd4 = as.numeric(date - last_cd4_date),

Packages

title: 6. Cohort
text:
Start at the first regimen
Days before the first regimen are dropped. Each patient’s initial regimen, and whether it was twice daily, is that of regimen 1. Stata generated the value on regimen-1 days and used carryforward to copy it down; taking it from regimen 1 directly gives the same value on every row.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Days before the first regimen are dropped. The first observation of a patient
# is the first day of regimen 1.
cohort_days <- analytic_days |>
  filter(!is.na(regimen_number)) |>
  left_join(baseline, by = "studyid") |>

section: Still in care and virologically suppressed
text:
Still in care and virologically suppressed
Still in care (lab-based): both a CD4 and a viral load are still to come. After a patient’s last test of either kind, they count as out of care.
Virologically suppressed: see vl_suppressed_on_day(). A day counts only if the most recent viral load is 400 or less. That result then counts for 90 days. A later day also counts if the next viral load comes within 90 days and is 400 or less too, which bridges a gap between two suppressed results. A suppressed result never reaches back to the days before it.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Still in care: a CD4 and a viral load are both still to come. Virologically
# suppressed: see vl_suppressed_on_day() in functions.R.
analytic_days <- daily |>
  left_join(day_coverage, by = c("studyid", "date")) |>
  mutate(
    still_in_care_cd4vl = !is.na(days_until_next_cd4) & !is.na(days_until_next_vl),
    vl_suppressed = vl_suppressed_on_day(lvcf_vl, days_since_last_vl,
                                         days_until_next_vl, next_vl,
                                         vl_suppression_main, lab_window_days)
  )

Viral suppression on a day
The daily definition used throughout. In Stata, a missing value is larger than any number, so missing <= 400 is false; coalesce(..., FALSE) gives R the same answer where R would otherwise return NA.


Click to show/hide R Code
# A day counts as virologically suppressed when the last viral load was at or
# below the threshold and it was either measured within the last 90 days, or the
# next one comes within 90 days and is also at or below the threshold (Stata
# Step 8). Stata treats comparisons with missing values as false; coalesce()
# does the same here.
vl_suppressed_on_day <- function(last_vl, days_since_last_vl, days_until_next_vl,
                                 next_vl, threshold, window_days) {
  suppressed <- last_vl <= threshold &
    (days_since_last_vl <= window_days |
       (days_until_next_vl <= window_days & next_vl <= threshold))
  coalesce(suppressed, FALSE)
}

The R counterparts of tab ..., chi2, ttest and ranksum, with the options that match Stata’s defaults. Used by 7. Propensity score.

# Baseline comparison between the STR and multi-tablet groups, as the Stata
# tab ..., chi2 / ttest / ranksum commands did. Stata's chi2 has no continuity
# correction, ttest assumes equal variances and ranksum uses the normal
# approximation.
compare_categorical <- function(patients, variable) {
  counts <- table(patients[[variable]], patients$str)
  tibble(variable = variable, test = "Pearson chi-squared",
         p_value = chisq.test(counts, correct = FALSE)$p.value)
}

compare_continuous <- function(patients, variable) {
  values <- patients[[variable]]
  t_test <- t.test(values ~ patients$str, var.equal = TRUE)
  rank_test <- wilcox.test(values ~ patients$str, exact = FALSE, correct = FALSE)
  tibble(
    variable = variable,
    test = c("t-test", "Wilcoxon rank-sum"),
    p_value = c(t_test$p.value, rank_test$p.value)
  )
}

title: Functions
text:
Odds ratios
The R counterpart of logistic outcome InitialRegimenSTR and logistic outcome InitialRegimenSTR [pw=IPW]. A probability-weighted logistic regression in Stata reports robust (sandwich) standard errors; svyglm() with a one-stage design and the weights gives the same kind. Confidence intervals are Wald intervals, as Stata’s are. Used by 8 and 9.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Odds ratio for an outcome comparing STR with multi-tablet regimens.
# Without weights: ordinary logistic regression (Stata: logistic y str).
# With weights: survey-weighted logistic regression, which gives the robust
# standard errors Stata reports for [pw=IPW].
odds_ratio_for_str <- function(patients, outcome, weight = NULL) {
  model_formula <- reformulate("str", response = outcome)
  model_data <- patients |> filter(!is.na(.data[[outcome]]))
  if (is.null(weight)) {
    model <- glm(model_formula, data = model_data, family = binomial())
    label <- "Unadjusted"
  } else {
    model_data <- model_data |> filter(!is.na(.data[[weight]]))
    design <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = reformulate(weight), data = model_data)
    model <- svyglm(model_formula, design = design, family = quasibinomial())
    label <- str_c("Weighted (", weight, ")")
  }
  # Wald confidence intervals and z-test p-values on the log-odds scale, as
  # Stata reports (svyglm's own p-values use the t distribution).
  tidy(model) |>
    filter(term == "strTRUE") |>
    transmute(outcome = outcome, analysis = label, patients = nrow(model_data),
              odds_ratio = exp(estimate),
              conf_low = exp(estimate - qnorm(0.975) * std.error),
              conf_high = exp(estimate + qnorm(0.975) * std.error),
              p_value = 2 * pnorm(-abs(estimate / std.error)))
}

Final Analysis and the paper
Final Analysis.do matches the paper (Hemmige et al. 2018): the three regimens compared (Atripla against darunavir or atazanavir boosted with ritonavir, each with Truvada), insurance in the propensity model, and psychiatry visits and a 50 copies/mL threshold as sensitivity analyses. Where the code is more specific than the paper
The code is the record of what was done, so these are kept as they are in both the Stata and the R:

Patients with prior care elsewhere and patients with no insurance status are excluded.
Viral suppression is 400 copies/mL or less, not less than 400.

title: Which file does what
text:
Slips in the code

Follow-up window. The saved file computes five outcomes over all of a patient’s days to the end of 2013, not the first year: regimen change (lines 63-64), suppression on the initial regimen (161-162), the proportion of days covered (167), days covered on the initial regimen (196-197), and the 50 copies/mL suppression (177). Each is a by studyid: egen with nothing limiting it to year one, unlike retention and year-one suppression, which go through Quarter. The 2015 version of the same calculations ran after keep if DaysSinceARTInitiation<365, which is missing here; Final Analysis.do was run by hand, and the R assumes that step was run but not saved. The paper reports these as first-year outcomes, so the R computes them for year one (step 8).
The models meant to use the psychiatry-adjusted weights (IPW2) use IPW. The R uses IPW2 (step 9).
(CurrentDrug4CurrentDispense) is missing its ==30. It does no harm, because the value is always 0 or 30.

Privacy
The do-files here are copies with patient-level details removed. Nothing else was changed.

Manual corrections. Step 0B had 576 lines correcting individual patients’ regimens, 396 of them for a specific dispensing date or date range, and Step 1A five more. A study ID with an exact date is more than a de-identified data set may contain, so each block is replaced by a note saying how many lines were removed and what form they took.
Notes about individual patients. Comments naming a study ID are replaced by a one-line note.
Paths and names. A local folder path is replaced by "<your analysis folder>", and a person’s name in a comment by a description.
Stop lines. Lines that deliberately stopped a do-file partway are replaced by a comment.

text:
Other outcomes
Each by studyid: egen x = max(...) or mean(...) in Stata becomes one line of a per-patient summarise(). any() is the R counterpart of max() over a 0/1 variable.
Every outcome uses the first year, days 0-364, as the paper describes: the data are filtered to first_year before summarising. This is a deliberate departure from the saved Stata. Its egen lines for suppression on the initial regimen, days covered and regimen change ran over every one of a patient’s days to the end of 2013, so a patient who started in 2008 would contribute up to six years and one who started late in 2011 two, and every day after a patient stopped filling would count as uncovered. The 2015 version of the same code limited the data to the first year first; the saved file lacks that step (details).

# describes. The saved Final Analysis.do computes suppression on the initial
# regimen, the proportion of days covered and regimen change over all of a
# patient's days to the end of 2013, because its `by studyid: egen` lines have
# no first-year restriction; the 2015 version of the same code restricted the
# data to year one first. See the "Which file does what" page.
patient_outcomes <- cohort_days |>
  filter(first_year) |>
  group_by(studyid) |>
  summarise(
    vl_suppressed_year_one = any(vl_suppressed),
    vl_suppressed_on_initial_regimen = any(vl_suppressed & on_initial_regimen),
    proportion_days_covered = mean(day_covered),
    proportion_days_covered_initial = mean(day_covered & on_initial_regimen),
    changed_regimen = n_distinct(regimen_number) > 1,
    .groups = "drop"

title: Overview
text: This site teaches the code behind a published study by translating the original Stata analysis into R, step by step. The paper is Hemmige et al. (2018).

title: Overview
text:
Clinical background
Single-tablet regimens (STRs) combine a complete antiretroviral regimen in one pill taken once a day. When the study was done, the only first-line STR in wide use at the clinic was efavirenz/tenofovir/emtricitabine (Atripla); the usual alternatives were a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor (darunavir or atazanavir) taken with tenofovir/emtricitabine (Truvada), which is three pills once a day. The question was whether starting on one pill rather than three made a difference to staying in care and reaching an undetectable viral load in the first year. More on the clinical background page.

title: Overview
text:
What this analysis does
It uses pharmacy fills, CD4 counts and viral loads from Thomas Street Health Center, a Harris Health System HIV clinic in Houston, for patients starting antiretroviral therapy (ART) in 2008-2011. It compares patients who started Atripla with those who started a boosted protease inhibitor with Truvada, on retention in care, viral suppression and medication coverage.

title: Overview
text:
Methods
Every patient becomes one row per day from 2008 to 2013, and each day records the regimen, whether pills were on hand, and the most recent labs. Outcomes are then compared between the two groups with and without inverse probability of treatment weights from a propensity score. Study design and methods explains each step in plain language, and the analysis plan is the formal specification.

title: Overview
text:
How to use this site

Code pages follow the R scripts in the order R/main.R runs them. Each one explains a step and shows the R code next to the Stata it replaces.
Original Stata code shows the do-files behind the paper as they were, with patient-level details removed, and how they fit together.

title: Overview
text:
Status
Teaching material for a completed, published study. The R code has been run only on synthetic data; it has not been used to reproduce the published numbers, and no real data or results from it are in this repository.

title: 7. Propensity score and weights
text:
Propensity model
The covariates are those listed in the paper. In Stata, Gender was the numbered category made by encode (1 = F, 2 = M) entered as a number, which is the same model as a male indicator. Patients missing any covariate, for example with no viral load before ART, get no score and so no weight, and drop out of the weighted analyses, as they did in Stata.
One difference to know about: if a category predicts the regimen perfectly (every patient in it started the STR, say), Stata’s logistic drops that category and its patients with a note, so they get no score and no weight. glm() keeps them, warns that fitted probabilities are numerically 0 or 1, and reports a huge coefficient and standard error for that category. Those patients’ own weights are not large: each received the regimen predicted for them, so the weight is close to 1. The difference is who is weighted, so the two programs can give different results. Check for the warning before using the weights.


Click to show/hide R Code
# The probability of starting an STR given the covariates listed in the paper.
# Patients missing any covariate get no propensity score and drop out of the
# weighted analyses, as in Stata.
propensity_model <- glm(
  str ~ hepc + male + black + hispanic + idu + msm + age_group +
    baseline_vl_group + baseline_cd4_group + insurance_category_3,
  data = patients, family = binomial()
)

title: 7. Propensity score and weights

Weights
Stata:
predict PropensityScore, p
generate IPW=(InitialRegimenSTR/PropensityScore)+(1-InitialRegimenSTR)/(1-PropensityScore)
The formula picks 1/p for STR patients and 1/(1-p) for the others; if_else() says so directly. These are average-treatment-effect weights.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Inverse probability of treatment weights: 1 / P(STR) for STR patients and
# 1 / P(multi-tablet) for the others.
patients <- patients |>
  mutate(
    propensity_score = predict(propensity_model, newdata = patients, type = "response"),
    ipw = if_else(str, 1 / propensity_score, 1 / (1 - propensity_score))
  )

The project
A teaching repository for a published study Hemmige et al., AIDS Care 2018 comparing single-tablet with multi-tablet first-line antiretroviral regimens at Thomas Street Health Center (Harris Health System). The original Stata code is in stata/ with patient-level details removed; R/ is a translation into R, run only on synthetic data. The code and methods are explained on a Quarto website. The study is complete: the R is not used to rerun the published analysis.

analysis-plan.md is the source of truth for design. It was reconstructed from the paper and the code. The code is the record of what was done; the plan marks where it is more specific than the paper’s methods. The R translation follows the code, except where the saved Stata is evidently a slip against the published method (for example, outcomes the paper reports for year one that the saved file computes over all follow-up); there the R follows the paper. Every such departure is stated on the script’s page and in stata_overview.qmd.
Deciders. Scientific decisions are made by: Vagish Hemmige (all areas). Anyone may open or contribute to an issue; only a decider settles it.
This is an analysis project, not an R package. Do not add DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, roxygen, or pkgdown infrastructure, or apply CRAN conventions.
Default branch: main, protected. Changes reach it only through pull requests.

Exploration is welcome on branches or forks. Experimental scripts need not be sourced from R/main.R or have Quarto pages. A script becomes part of the definitive translation when it is sourced from R/main.R; from then on every rule below applies to it. R/synthetic/ is a utility, not part of the definitive workflow.

R scripts

Running the code. Run R/synthetic/make_synthetic_data.R, then R/main.R, from the project root. main.R sources the other scripts in dependency order; ARCHITECTURE.md describes what each does.
One job per script. When you add a definitive script, source it from main.R at the right point and update ARCHITECTURE.md in the same pull request.
Header comment. Each script begins with what it does, the Stata it translates, which objects it needs from earlier scripts, and what it produces.
Constants, libraries, and code lists live in R/setup.R. Other scripts do not call library(), re-source setup.R, or hard-code values.
Helper functions go in R/functions.R. A function takes its inputs as arguments and does not read global objects.
No side effects outside the project. No setwd(), absolute paths, or writes outside the project.
No results in the repository. No script, comment, commit message, issue, pull-request text or review report contains results, counts or data values from the real data. Synthetic results are never described as results.

Chunk labels
Scripts are divided into labelled sections so Quarto pages can show the code without copying it:
## ---- <step-name>

Every logical step has a label. A label covers the code from its line to the next label.
Labels are kebab-case, describe the step, and are unique across all scripts; a duplicate silently picks up the wrong code.
Search the .qmd files before renaming or deleting a label.

Quarto website
The site documents the code. It does not run the analysis.

_quarto.yml, index.qmd, 404.qmd and styles.css sit at the root; quarto/ has one page per definitive script, named after it, the Stata pages, and the Background, Study design and methods, About and project-document pages. The custom-callout extension in _extensions/ provides the Rcode, Results and Pending callouts.
Visual cues. Background book (blue); study design and methods diagram-3 (orange); R code, including the Stata pages, laptop (pink, Rcode 💻); results clipboard-data (green); project documents file-earmark-ruled (grey).
Provisional content. quarto/_pending.lua highlights in yellow every paragraph that starts with Decision pending: or, in the plan, Open:, and any [text]{.pending}.
Project documents. analysis-plan.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, AGENTS.md and REPOSITORY-BLUEPRINT.md are shown by pages in quarto/ that only include the root file: edit the root file, not the page.
Each script page loads its script with knitr::read_chunk("../R/<script>.R") and shows each labelled section with #| eval: false, with prose explaining what it does, why, and the Stata it replaces.
Chunks that run: the read_chunk() imports, the Architecture page’s chunk that reads ARCHITECTURE.md, and the chunks that show the do-files through quarto/_stata_links.R, which read stata/ and quarto/stata_map.csv as text. Nothing else is evaluated.
The site renders to docs/, which is not committed: the GitHub Actions workflow .github/workflows/publish.yml renders it and publishes it to the gh-pages branch on every push to main. When you add a script, add its page and sidebar entry in the same pull request, and render locally to check it.
Prose must match the code. If a change alters what a section does, update its explanation in the same pull request.

The Stata code

stata/ holds the original do-files with patient-level details removed (stata/README.md lists what was removed). Do not add study IDs, person-level dates, local paths or notes about individual patients back.
The do-files are a record and are not edited otherwise, including their bugs, which are documented on the site’s “Which file does what” page (quarto/stata_overview.qmd).
Stata-R links. quarto/stata_map.csv splits each do-file into sections (line ranges) and names the R chunk labels that replace each one. The Stata pages and the folded “Stata:” blocks under each R step are both built from it. When you rename, add or remove a chunk label, update the map in the same pull request, and keep every non-blank do-file line in exactly one section.

Outputs

R/tables.R writes to tables/, which is gitignored: tables from synthetic data mean nothing, and tables from the real data would need clearing before release. There are no figures.
README.Rmd is the source of README.md; edit the .Rmd and re-knit.

Restricted data (applies to everyone)

Never commit data, extracts, the manual corrections, or anything derived from patient-level records.
AI agents never read restricted data. Agents write code, review it, and run it on synthetic data only.
Synthetic data are built in code, labelled as synthetic, and never derived from real records.
Disclosure. No study IDs, person-level dates or small cells from the real data in any file, comment, commit message, issue or pull request.

Coding conventions

Faithful translation first. Each R step reproduces what the Stata did, including choices the paper does not mention. Where the saved Stata is a slip against the published method (the psychiatry weights, the year-one window), the R follows the paper, and the script comment and its page say so.
Cohort flow: exclusions go through count_patients() in R/06_cohort.R in the plan’s order, so the flow counts and the cohort come from the same code.
Joins state a relationship where rows could multiply.
Style: readable for a clinician-analyst who learned R from online guides: pipes and dplyr/tidyr verbs, case_when(), loops over names or named lists. Required base R (the day-by-day pill count) is in named functions in R/functions.R.

Checks for any change

Fidelity: does the R still do what the Stata does, and is every departure documented?
Structure: is ARCHITECTURE.md current; are chunk labels unique and found by their pages; does every definitive script have a page and sidebar entry?
Disclosure: search every changed file, commit message and pull-request text for study IDs, dates, names and paths.
Execution: do R/synthetic/make_synthetic_data.R and R/main.R run in a fresh session; does the site render?

Working with agents

Autonomy. The person directing an agent sets its working style in their own instructions. At most, an agent may edit code and documentation, run code and render the site on synthetic data, and commit to a branch and open a pull request.
Every agent, under any autonomy: never merges a pull request; follows the restricted-data rules; shows a person the exact text before posting anything as them.
References: cite sources in references.bib.

text: This script runs the sensitivity analyses the paper reports: a lower viral load threshold after 2008, a propensity model that adds psychiatry visits, and excluding patients who may have filled their prescriptions elsewhere.

title: 9. Sensitivity analyses
text:
A lower threshold after 2008
The assay changed after 2008, so patients who started later are held to 50 copies/mL. The same daily rule is reused with a threshold that depends on the year ART started, and results are tabulated by start year, as the Stata did one tab ... if YearofARTInitiation==2008 line at a time.
As in the main analysis, suppression is counted in the first year; the saved Stata took it over all follow-up (details).


Click to show/hide R Code
# 400 copies/mL for patients starting ART in 2008 and 50 copies/mL afterwards,
# applied to the year-one suppression outcome as the paper describes. (The saved
# Stata takes the maximum over all follow-up.)
suppression_by_year_threshold <- cohort_days |>
  filter(first_year) |>
  mutate(
    threshold = if_else(art_start_year == 2008, vl_suppression_main, vl_suppression_later),
    vl_suppressed_year_threshold = vl_suppressed_on_day(
      lvcf_vl, days_since_last_vl, days_until_next_vl, next_vl,
      threshold, lab_window_days
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(studyid) |>
  summarise(vl_suppressed_year_threshold = any(vl_suppressed_year_threshold),
            .groups = "drop")

patients <- patients |>
  left_join(suppression_by_year_threshold, by = "studyid")

suppression_by_start_year <- patients |>
  group_by(art_start_year, str) |>
  summarise(patients = n(), suppressed = sum(vl_suppressed_year_threshold),
            percent = 100 * suppressed / patients, .groups = "drop")

title: 9. Sensitivity analyses
section: Adding psychiatry visits to the propensity model
text:
Adding psychiatry visits to the propensity model
First, whether patients with a psychiatry visit were less likely to start the STR, as prescribers may avoid efavirenz in psychiatric illness. Then update() refits the propensity model with one more term.
R departs from the Stata: Final Analysis.do computed the new weights (IPW2) but its next two models were written with [pw=IPW], the original weights. The R uses the new weights, which is what the paper describes. Anyone comparing with the Stata log should expect these two models to differ.


Click to show/hide R Code
# The paper reports that adding psychiatry clinic visits to the propensity
# model did not meaningfully change the odds ratios. Final Analysis.do computed
# these weights (IPW2) but its next two models used the original weights; here
# the new weights are used, as the paper describes.
# Stata: tab InitialRegimenSTR HadPsychDate if FirstObs, row column chi2
psych_test <- compare_categorical(patients, "had_psych_visit")

propensity_model_psych <- update(propensity_model, . ~ . + had_psych_visit)

patients <- patients |>
  mutate(
    propensity_score_psych = predict(propensity_model_psych, newdata = patients,
                                     type = "response"),
    ipw_psych = if_else(str, 1 / propensity_score_psych, 1 / (1 - propensity_score_psych))
  )

psych_models <- bind_rows(
  odds_ratio_for_str(patients, "retained_year_one", weight = "ipw_psych"),
  odds_ratio_for_str(patients, "vl_suppressed_year_one", weight = "ipw_psych")
)

title: 9. Sensitivity analyses
text:
Possible outside pharmacy
A suppressed viral load measured 90 or more days after the last fill of a drug in the current regimen suggests the patient was getting medication somewhere else. Stata counted days since the last fill with the same running-sum trick used for labs; here the last fill date is filled down and subtracted. A patient is flagged if this happens at any time in follow-up, and the flag is compared between the groups.


Click to show/hide R Code
# A suppressed viral load (<= 400) measured 90 or more days after the last fill
# of a drug in the current regimen suggests medication from another pharmacy.
# Stata treats a missing "days since" (no fill yet on the current regimen) as
# larger than 90, so such a day can be flagged; coalesce(..., TRUE) does the same.
fill_gaps <- cohort_days |>
  arrange(studyid, date) |>
  mutate(last_dispense_date = if_else(any_drug_dispensed, date, as.Date(NA))) |>
  group_by(studyid) |>
  fill(last_dispense_date, .direction = "down") |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    days_since_last_dispense = as.numeric(date - last_dispense_date),
    suppressed_without_fill = coalesce(current_vl <= vl_suppression_main, FALSE) &
      coalesce(days_since_last_dispense >= missed_fill_days, TRUE)
  )

outside_pharmacy <- fill_gaps |>
  group_by(studyid) |>
  summarise(possible_outside_pharmacy = any(suppressed_without_fill), .groups = "drop")

patients <- patients |>
  left_join(outside_pharmacy, by = "studyid")

# Stata: tab SwitchesPharmacy InitialRegimenSTR if FirstObservationOfSubject, chi2
outside_pharmacy_summary <- patients |>
  count(str, possible_outside_pharmacy)
outside_pharmacy_test <- compare_categorical(patients, "possible_outside_pharmacy")

title: Study design and methods
text: This page explains, in plain language and without code, what this study chose and why. The general background is on Methodological background. The formal specification is the analysis plan; each section links the part of the plan that governs it. Two kinds of note mark where the description stands:

title: Study design and methods
section: The question and the design in brief
text:
The question and the design in brief
A retrospective cohort of treatment-naive patients who started ART at Thomas Street Health Center between 2008 and 2011, comparing those who started the single-tablet regimen Atripla with those who started a boosted protease inhibitor with Truvada. Outcomes are measured in the first year after the first fill; the comparison is reported as odds ratios, unadjusted and weighted by the inverse probability of treatment.
Specified in: §1 Objective and §2 Design.

title: Study design and methods
text:
Working out each patient’s regimen
The pharmacy record lists every drug dispensed. The drugs filled on the same day are joined into a regimen name (for example Norvir/Prezista/Truvada), and a new regimen starts whenever that name changes. This simple rule fails when a patient picks up only part of a regimen on a given day, so the original analyst reviewed the patients whose sequences looked wrong and wrote 576 manual corrections. Those corrections name individual patients and dates, so they are not published; the R code shows how such corrections are applied using a made-up example.
A regimen is classed as twice daily if any drug in it was dispensed as a twice-daily product (for example raltegravir or lopinavir/ritonavir). Early Complera fills recorded as Truvada were recoded.
Specified in: §5 Exposure and time zero.

title: Study design and methods
text:
The person-day data set
Every patient gets one row per day from 1 January 2008 to 31 December 2013. Each day carries the current regimen, the CD4 and viral load measured that day if any, the last values carried forward, and the days since the last and until the next test.

title: Study design and methods
text:
Medication on hand
Every fill is assumed to be 30 pills. For each drug, pills on hand go up by 30 on a fill day and down by one each day; early refills add to what is left, and pills of a drug carried into a new regimen that contains it count. A day is covered when every drug in the current regimen is on hand.
Specified in: §7 Outcomes.

title: Study design and methods
text:
Who is included
Patients are included if their first regimen is one of the three compared regimens and is taken once daily. Time zero is the first day of the first regimen.
Enrollment and follow-up are different windows. Patients started ART in 2008-2011; the data then follow them to the end of 2013, so everyone has a full first year. The code enforces only the start of enrollment, because a regimen begun before 2008 is not on the day-by-day grid. The end of enrollment, 2011, is not in the kept code; it is assumed to come from how the data extract was drawn.
From the code: no upper limit on the ART start date; the extract is assumed to have supplied it.
Specified in: §4 Study population.
From the code: the code also excludes patients recorded as having had prior care elsewhere, and patients with no insurance status; the paper’s methods do not mention either exclusion.

title: Study design and methods
text:
Outcomes

Retention in care in year one: at least two viral loads in days 0-364 after the first fill, more than 90 days apart.
Viral suppression in year one: at least one day in days 0-364 on which the patient counts as suppressed: the last viral load was 400 copies/mL or less, and either it was measured within the last 90 days or the next one, within 90 days, was also 400 or less.
Suppression on the initial regimen: suppressed on a day while still on the first regimen.
Adherence: proportion of days covered of 80% or more in the first year.

R departs from the Stata: every outcome is measured in the first year. The saved Stata file computed some of them over all follow-up, a step assumed run but not saved (details).
Specified in: §7 Outcomes.
From the code: suppression is defined as 400 copies/mL or less; the paper’s text says less than 400.

title: Study design and methods
text:
Comparing the groups
A logistic regression gives each patient’s probability of starting the STR from hepatitis C, sex, Black race, Hispanic ethnicity, injection drug use, men who have sex with men, age group, baseline viral load group, baseline CD4 group and insurance. Each patient is weighted by the inverse of the probability of the regimen they started. Each outcome is compared with logistic regression, without weights and with them (robust standard errors).
Specified in: §8 Statistical analysis.

title: Study design and methods
text:
Sensitivity analyses

A viral load threshold of 50 copies/mL for patients starting after 2008.
A propensity model that also includes any psychiatry visit.
Excluding patients who had a suppressed viral load 90 or more days after their last fill, which suggests they were filling elsewhere.

Specified in: §9 Sensitivity analyses.
R departs from the Stata: in the saved Stata, the models meant to use the weights from the psychiatry propensity model use the main weights instead. The R uses the new weights, as the paper describes.

title: 1. Regimens from pharmacy fills
text: This script turns the pharmacy dispensing record into each patient’s sequence of regimens, with the date each one started and whether it is taken twice daily. It produces fills and regimen_episodes for 4. Daily regimen.

section: Fix drug names and flag twice-daily products
text:
Fix drug names and flag twice-daily products
Some fills were recorded as “Experimental” or “Other” though the product description shows the drug. A join to the lookup table in setup.R replaces six Stata replace lines. Each fill is also flagged if its product is taken twice a day: for example, darunavir 600 mg is the twice-daily dose, while 800 mg (two 400 mg tablets) is the once-daily dose.


Click to show/hide R Code
fills <- fills_raw |>
  left_join(drug_name_fixes, by = "cdmdescription") |>
  mutate(
    drugname = coalesce(fixed_drugname, drugname),
    dispense_date = mdy(medtransdate),
    bid_drug = cdmdescription %in% bid_descriptions
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(drugname), drugname != "") |>
  select(studyid, dispense_date, drugname, cdmdescription, bid_drug)

title: 1. Regimens from pharmacy fills
section: Name the regimen on each fill date
text:
Name the regimen on each fill date
The drugs filled on the same day, sorted alphabetically and joined with “/”, make that day’s regimen name. In Stata this took a reshape wide by drug, a loop to paste the names together, a string trick to trim trailing slashes, and a reshape long back:
bysort studyid DispenseNumber ( drugname) : generate M=_n
reshape wide drugname cdmcode cdmdescription cdpdrugcode drugconstituents BIDDrug , i( studyid DispenseNumber ) j( M)
generate CurrentRegimen=drugname1
forvalue i=2(1)$SizeOfLargestRegimen {
replace CurrentRegimen=CurrentRegimen+"/"+ drugname`i'
}
In R it is a grouped summary.


Click to show/hide R Code
dispense_regimens <- fills |>
  group_by(studyid, dispense_date) |>
  summarise(regimen = make_regimen_name(drugname), .groups = "drop")





Stata: Do Step 0B Current Regimen.do, lines 25-34 (Number each patient’s fill dates)

See it in context
//Now, we generate a variable DispenseNumber that keeps a running total of how many unique dispense dates
//each patient has, after sorting and creating a variable NewDispense which labels the first dispense for every pt and unique date:
sort studyid ARTDate drugname
by studyid: generate N=_n
generate NewDispense=0
by studyid: replace NewDispense=1 if ((N>1)&( ARTDate[_n]>ARTDate[_n-1]))
replace NewDispense=1 if N==1
by studyid: generate DispenseNumber=sum(NewDispense)
drop NewDispense
drop N



Stata: Do Step 0B Current Regimen.do, lines 42-59 (Name the regimen on each fill date)

See it in context
//We now create a string variable CurrentRegimen which contains the current regimen on that date based on medications filled on that date
bysort studyid DispenseNumber ( drugname) : generate M=_n
quietly summarize M
global SizeOfLargestRegimen `r(max)' //Stores the maximum number of drugs any patient is taking simultaneously

//Now we reshape wide based on number of drugs dispensed on a date
reshape wide drugname cdmcode cdmdescription cdpdrugcode drugconstituents BIDDrug , i( studyid DispenseNumber ) j( M)

//The following loop creates the variable CurrentRegimen by adding together the various drugnames for any given date
generate CurrentRegimen=drugname1
forvalue i=2(1)$SizeOfLargestRegimen {
replace CurrentRegimen=CurrentRegimen+"/"+ drugname`i'
}
replace CurrentRegimen = reverse(substr(reverse(CurrentRegimen), indexnot(reverse(CurrentRegimen), "/"), .)) //Trims unnecessary /'s at end of line
//Now we reshape wide so that each row is a single drug dispensed on a single date
reshape long drugname cdmcode cdmdescription cdpdrugcode drugconstituents BIDDrug, i( studyid DispenseNumber ) j( M)
drop M
drop if drugname==""

title: 1. Regimens from pharmacy fills
text:
Number the regimens
A new regimen starts on the first fill date and on any fill date whose regimen name differs from the one before. A regimen is twice daily if any fill within it was a twice-daily product. One row per regimen remains, with its start date; Stata kept the same by keep if NewRegimen and reshaped it wide with one column per regimen.


Click to show/hide R Code
# A new regimen starts on any fill date whose regimen name differs from the
# previous fill date's. A regimen is twice daily if any fill in it is a
# twice-daily product.
regimen_episodes <- fills |>
  group_by(studyid, dispense_date, regimen) |>
  summarise(bid_dispense = any(bid_drug), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(studyid, dispense_date) |>
  group_by(studyid) |>
  mutate(
    new_regimen = regimen != lag(regimen, default = ""),
    regimen_number = cumsum(new_regimen)
  ) |>
  group_by(studyid, regimen_number) |>
  summarise(
    regimen = first(regimen),
    regimen_start = first(dispense_date),
    bid_regimen = any(bid_dispense),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

See it in context
//We now create a file which contains one line for each new regimen and the start date.
//The maximum number of new regimens per subject is saved in the global $MaxNumberRegimens

bysort studyid (ARTDate): generate N=_n
generate NewRegimen=0
replace NewRegimen=1 if N==1
by studyid: replace NewRegimen=1 if ((N>1)&( CurrentRegimen[_n]~=CurrentRegimen[_n-1]))
by studyid: generate RegimenNumber=sum(NewRegimen)
quietly summarize RegimenNumber

display "Maximum number of regimens: " $MaxNumberRegimens

//Now we write code that labels whether dispenses or regimens are BID:
bysort studyid DispenseNumber: egen BIDDispense=max(BIDDrug) //Labels each dispense as being BID or not
bysort studyid RegimenNumber: egen BIDRegimen=max(BIDDrug) //Labels each new regimen as BID

Scope and reporting framework
This document is the authoritative specification of the study’s scientific objectives, population, definitions, estimands and statistical methods. ARCHITECTURE.md documents the implementation, AGENTS.md the working conventions, and GitHub Issues any open questions. Neither file supersedes this plan.
The code is the record of what was done. Where it is more specific than the paper’s methods, this plan states what the code does, marked From the code.
Reporting followed STROBE (Elm et al. 2007); RECORD (Benchimol et al. 2015) applies to studies of routinely collected data like this one. The reporting map below links checklist items to sections of this plan.

1. Objective
To compare, among treatment-naive patients starting antiretroviral therapy (ART), a single-tablet regimen (STR) with a once-daily multi-tablet regimen (MTR) on:

Primary: retention in care and viral suppression in the first year.
Secondary: viral suppression while on the initial regimen; adherence measured as proportion of days covered (PDC).

Hypothesis stated in advance: STR is associated with better retention and suppression.

2. Design
Retrospective cohort study using routinely collected clinic pharmacy and laboratory data. The comparison is observational; confounding by measured characteristics is addressed with inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), targeting the average treatment effect in the cohort. Target-trial emulation was not used.

3. Data source
Thomas Street Health Center, Harris Health System, Houston, Texas. De-identified extracts, prepared for the study, of:

Antiretroviral dispensing from the clinic pharmacy (drug, product description, date).
CD4 counts and HIV-1 viral loads (date, numeric result).
Demographics and HIV transmission risk at intake.
Insurance status and prior HIV care elsewhere at intake.
Psychiatry clinic visit dates.

Enrollment and follow-up are separate:

Enrollment: patients starting ART from 1 January 2008 to 31 December 2011 (Hemmige et al. 2018). This restriction is not in the kept code: Final Analysis.do applies no upper limit to the start date (it tabulates a 2012 start year). It is assumed to come from how the extract was drawn; the paper reports 2,095 patients entering care in the period.
Follow-up: the person-day data run to 31 December 2013, so every enrolled patient has a full first year. Each outcome uses days 0-364 after the first fill (§7).

The data are not public and are not in this repository.

4. Study population
Source population: patients in the extract with antiretrovirals dispensed by the clinic pharmacy. The code enforces the start of enrollment indirectly: a patient whose first regimen started before 1 January 2008 has no first regimen on the person-day grid and is dropped at exclusion 1.
Exclusions, in order (each a flowchart step):

Initial regimen in the window is taken twice daily (any twice-daily product), or the first regimen started before the window.
Initial regimen is not one of: Atripla; Norvir/Prezista/Truvada; Norvir/Reyataz/Truvada.
Recorded as having had HIV care elsewhere, or that field missing. From the code: the paper’s methods do not mention this exclusion.
Insurance status missing. From the code: the paper’s methods do not mention this exclusion.

Index event (time zero): the first day of the first regimen (first fill).

5. Exposure and time zero
Regimen. On each fill date, the drugs dispensed are joined, in alphabetical order, into a regimen name. The original analyst manually corrected the regimen on specific fill dates where only part of a regimen was filled (576 corrections in the final code; not published). A Truvada fill on a date whose regimen is Complera is recoded as Complera. A new regimen starts on any fill date whose regimen name differs from the previous fill date’s. A regimen is twice daily if any fill within it is a twice-daily product (list in R/setup.R).
Exposure. STR: initial regimen Atripla (efavirenz/tenofovir/emtricitabine). MTR: initial regimen Norvir/Prezista/Truvada or Norvir/Reyataz/Truvada (ritonavir-boosted darunavir or atazanavir with tenofovir/emtricitabine). Intention to treat: classified by initial regimen regardless of later switches.
Covariates, measured at time zero:

Age (groups: <25, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65+), sex, Black race, Hispanic ethnicity, injection drug use, men who have sex with men, hepatitis C, insurance (the third insurance category in the extract; described in the paper as insured vs uninsured).
Baseline viral load: last value on or before time zero (groups: 0-400, 401-999, 1,000-9,999, 10,000-99,999, 100,000-999,999, 1,000,000+ copies/mL).
Baseline CD4: last value on or before time zero (groups: <50, 50-99, 100-199, 200-499, 500+ cells/µL).
Any psychiatry visit on file (sensitivity analysis only).

6. Comparator or matching
No matching. Comparison by IPTW: weights 1/p for STR patients and 1/(1-p) for MTR patients, where p is the propensity score (§8).

7. Outcomes
Daily measures, on a grid of one row per patient per day:

Pills on hand, per drug: every fill is 30 pills; +30 on a fill day, -1 per day, never below zero; a fill when none are left gives 30; pills of the same drug carry into a new regimen.
Day covered: every drug in the current regimen on hand.
Virologically suppressed on a day: last viral load ≤400 copies/mL and either measured within the previous 90 days, or the next viral load is within 90 days and also ≤400. From the code: the paper’s text says <400.

Patient outcomes:

Retention in care, year one: at least two viral loads in days 0-364 after time zero, more than 90 days apart (HRSA-style definition using viral load tests).
Viral suppression, year one: suppressed on at least one day in days 0-364.
Viral suppression on the initial regimen: suppressed on at least one day in days 0-364 while on the initial regimen.
Adherence: PDC ≥ 0.80, with PDC the proportion of days 0-364 covered.
Adherence on the initial regimen: proportion of days 0-364 that are both covered and on the initial regimen ≥ 0.80.
Regimen change: any change of regimen in days 0-364 (descriptive); suppression on the day of the first switch.

All patient outcomes use days 0-364. The saved Do Final Analysis.do computes suppression on the initial regimen, both adherence measures and the 50 copies/mL sensitivity outcome over all follow-up to 31 December 2013; the 2015 version of the same calculations restricted the data to the first year, as the paper reports. This plan follows the paper.

8. Statistical analysis

Descriptive: baseline characteristics by group; Pearson chi-squared for categorical variables, t-test (equal variances) and Wilcoxon rank-sum for age, baseline viral load and CD4.
Propensity score: logistic regression of STR on hepatitis C, sex, Black race, Hispanic ethnicity, injection drug use, MSM, age group, baseline viral load group, baseline CD4 group and insurance. Patients missing a covariate receive no weight and are excluded from weighted analyses.
Balance: weighted proportions and means by group.
Outcome models: for each outcome, logistic regression on STR, unadjusted and IPTW-weighted with robust standard errors. Odds ratios with Wald 95% confidence intervals.
Missing data: complete cases for each model.
Multiplicity: no adjustment.
Software: Stata 12 (original); R (this teaching translation).

9. Sensitivity analyses

Assay threshold: suppression defined with ≤50 copies/mL for patients starting ART after 2008 (≤400 for 2008), tabulated by year of ART start. Tests whether the 400 cut-off, set by the 2008 assay, hides differences. Suppression is counted in days 0-364, as in the main analysis.
Psychiatric history: propensity model adding any psychiatry visit; retention and year-one suppression re-estimated with the new weights. Tests confounding by mental illness.
Outside pharmacy: excluding patients with a viral load ≤400 measured 90 or more days after their last fill of a drug in the current regimen, at any time in follow-up; main models re-estimated, unweighted and with the original weights. Tests whether fills elsewhere bias the outcomes.

10. Disclosure control
The data are clinic records under the study’s IRB approval and Harris Health policy. No patient-level data, study IDs, or person-level dates are published, including in code: the manual regimen corrections are kept with the data. Results are those published in the paper; no new results from the real data are released here.

11. Limitations to address in reporting

Observational design; unmeasured confounding, including clinicians’ choice of protease inhibitors for patients expected to adhere poorly.
The comparison mixes pill burden with drug class (efavirenz vs boosted protease inhibitors).
Pharmacy fills measure collection, not ingestion, and miss fills elsewhere: PDC is a lower bound.
Loss to follow-up cannot be distinguished from moving, transferring care, incarceration or death.
Single clinic serving a largely uninsured, racially diverse population.

title: Clinical background
text: Antiretroviral therapy works only if it is taken. Staying in care, collecting refills and taking pills every day are all harder for patients facing poverty, unstable housing, mental illness or substance use, which describes much of the population served by a county safety-net HIV clinic. One proposed help is to make the regimen simpler: a single tablet once a day rather than several.

Clinicians may also have chosen protease inhibitors for patients they expected to adhere poorly, because protease inhibitors are less prone to resistance. The paper discusses both limitations (Hemmige et al. 2018).

What the study found
Patients who started the STR were more likely to be retained in care and to reach viral suppression in the first year, after propensity weighting; differences in pharmacy-based adherence were small and not statistically significant (Hemmige et al. 2018). The numbers are in the paper; this site does not reproduce them.

R/synthetic/make_synthetic_data.R is a utility outside the workflow: it writes six CSVs and an example corrections file with the original column names, filled with random values.

Design choices in the translation

Long, not wide. Stata reshaped labs and fills to one row per patient with numbered columns, then looped over the numbers. R keeps one row per test, fill or drug and uses joins and grouped summaries.
One row per drug per day replaces Stata’s CurrentDrug1...6 columns, so coverage is all()/any() over a group.
A patient table (patients) replaces Stata’s if FirstObservationOfSubject on every command.
Loops only where each value depends on the previous one: pills on hand (count_pills_on_hand()), and processing regimens in order for the carry-over between them.
Manual corrections are data, read from a file, not code.
